title: Magnetic Chore Chart: DIY Reusable or Buy One? (Free PDF)
meta_description: A magnetic chore chart lives where the work happens. Here's how to DIY a reusable fridge version from a free printable, plus an honest buy-vs-DIY guide.
h1: Magnetic Chore Chart: DIY a Reusable Fridge Chart (or Buy One)
intro:
I'm Andrew, a dad of four, and in our house the charts that ever earned their keep were the ones stuck where the work actually happens — on the fridge, on a bedroom wall, down at kid eye-level. That's the honest case for a magnetic chore chart: not that a magnet motivates anyone (it doesn't), but that a board mounted on the fridge stays visible and stays put. A chore list living inside a parent's phone can't do that, which is a big part of why we've always been a print-it-and-post-it family, especially when the kids were little.

The good news is you don't need to buy a fancy board to get there. You can turn a free printable into a wipe-clean, magnet-backed chart in about ten minutes, and it'll do the job just as well as most store-bought versions. Below I'll walk through exactly how we'd make one, then give you a straight buy-vs-DIY comparison so you can decide what's actually worth your money — and how to make it work whether you've got one kid, four, or you're building one for yourself.

sections.heading: Why the fridge beats the phone (a chart is a parent's tracking tool)
sections.body:
Before you laminate anything, it helps to be clear about what a magnetic chore chart is really for. In our experience it's a tracking tool for the parents — a way to glance at the fridge and see who's keeping up and who needs a nudge — far more than it's a motivation gadget for the kids. The motivation in our home has never come from the chart itself. It comes from the plain expectation that chores belong to the whole family and everyone pitches in because this is our home. Rewards and screen time we deliberately keep on their own track; allowance exists, but it's tied to the overall picture — whether a kid is keeping up, doing careful work, and staying reasonably pleasant about it — not paid out task by task.

That's exactly why the fridge wins over an app. A chart taped up where the work happens is visible to the kids, all day, without anyone unlocking a phone. For our youngest that visibility is the whole point: a picture cue posted right at the spot a task happens — a little icon by the sink, or on the toy bin — tells a pre-reader what's next without a lecture. And kids are wired differently even under one roof. Our 9-year-old doesn't really register a chart at all; for him it's purely our tracking sheet, and the real work is done by telling him each step in real time. Our 11-year-old, meanwhile, genuinely loves a chart and lights up getting to design her own — which is a strong argument for a reusable, wipe-clean board she can redraw whenever she likes.

One more quiet benefit of a reusable board: it's easy to restart. Most systems don't fail because they were bad — they fail because a vacation or a rough week knocks them over and nobody rebuilds them. A dry-erase or swap-the-page chart wipes clean and resets in seconds, so a bad week doesn't become a dead chart.

sections.heading: How to DIY a reusable magnetic chore chart from a free printable
sections.body:
Start with a template you can reuse. Our free blank chore chart is built for exactly this, and if you want to change the categories or add each kid's name first, the editable chore chart lets you type it in before you print. Then pick the finish that fits how permanent you want it:

- Laminate it. Run the printed page through a laminator (or use self-seal laminating pouches — no machine needed). The plastic surface takes a dry-erase marker, so you can check off and wipe the same chart for months. This is the most durable option.
- Use a dry-erase pocket or sleeve. Slide the printout into a clear plastic sleeve. Cheaper than laminating, and the real advantage is you can pull the page out and swap it when your tasks change or your kid wants to redesign the whole thing.
- Make it magnetic. Stick adhesive magnet strips or magnetic tape to the back, drop it into a magnetic photo pocket, or clip it to a thin metal board. If your fridge is one of the stainless kinds that magnets won't grip, a cheap metal cookie sheet on the wall (or command strips straight onto the wall) gives you the same eye-level, always-visible spot.

For a magnetic chore chart for kids who can't read yet, lean on pictures over words and keep it to a few steps. For a magnetic chore chart for multiple kids, give each child their own column and their own marker color, or make small magnet tokens with each name that they physically move from "to do" to "done" — kids like the act of moving a piece, and you get a one-glance read on who's behind. Test your marker on a corner first; some "dry-erase" markers stain cheap laminate, and a fine-tip works better than a fat one on a small grid.

sections.heading: Buy vs. DIY: an honest comparison
sections.body:
I'll be straight with you: we don't have affiliate links on this page, and I'm not going to name products or quote prices I can't stand behind. What I can do is lay out the real trade-off so you can choose.

DIY (from the printable) is cheap, endlessly customizable, and restartable. You control the wording, the categories, and the layout, so it matches your family instead of forcing your family to match it. The downsides: it looks homemade, and you do have to spend a few minutes assembling it (and maybe buy pouches or magnet tape).

A store-bought magnetic chore chart is usually more durable and more polished, and it arrives with the pieces already made — magnets, a frame, pre-printed task tiles. If you want something that looks nice on the fridge and you'd rather not fiddle, buying is a reasonable call, and it saves you the setup. The catches: it costs more, its fixed categories may not fit your household, and — this is the part the product page won't tell you — the board doesn't do the parenting. A beautiful magnetic chart will get ignored by the same kid who'd ignore a paper one.

So the honest recommendation isn't "buy the fanciest board" or "never buy one." It's: spend on the board only if a nicer-looking, no-fuss version will actually get you to keep it up. The system is you checking the chart and following through — the chart is just where you keep score. Match the tool to your kid, not to the product photos.

sections.heading: Making it work for multiple kids, teens, and adults
sections.body:
Multiple kids: a single visible board scales well if you give each child a column, a color, or a name magnet, and keep the whole thing on the fridge where you'll actually see it. Resist the urge to make it elaborate — the more moving parts, the faster it dies. Its job is still to let you spot at a glance who needs a nudge.

By age, expectations shift. Little ones can't run a chart on their own; they need the visible cue plus you prompting the next step in the moment, and a heads-up before a transition ("in ten minutes we're doing the dishwasher") saves a lot of friction. Kids like our 11-year-old will happily own and redraw a dry-erase board — that's the sweet spot for a reusable chart. Teens tend to outgrow the family chart entirely; in our house that stage turned into more of a job-style arrangement than a fridge grid, and that's fine.

A magnetic chore chart for adults is a real use case, not a joke — it's basically how I keep myself on track. If your brain won't hold a task list, the fix is to get it out of your head and somewhere you can see it. A wipe-clean board on the fridge, or a sticky-note setup where you physically move a note from "to do" to "done," makes the size of the work visible and gives you the small hit of progress that keeps you moving. The same visible-where-you-live principle that helps the kids helps grown-ups too.

And one benefit I only fully appreciated during our fostering years: a routine posted where everyone can see it lets any adult in the house run the day the same way. It made handoffs painless — either of us could step in, glance at the fridge, and keep things consistent for kids who badly needed that consistency. For a busy or shared household, that alone can be worth the ten minutes it takes to make one.

faq.q: How do I make a magnetic chore chart?
faq.a: Print a reusable template (our free blank or editable chore chart works well), then either laminate it or slide it into a clear dry-erase pocket so it wipes clean. To make it magnetic, stick magnet tape or adhesive magnet strips to the back, or clip it to a thin metal board. If magnets won't grip your fridge, hang a cheap metal cookie sheet on the wall at kid eye-level and use that as your surface. The whole thing takes about ten minutes.

faq.q: Is it better to laminate the chart or use a dry-erase pocket?
faq.a: Both take a dry-erase marker, so it comes down to how often you'll change it. Laminating is more permanent and durable — good if your tasks are settled. A dry-erase pocket is cheaper and lets you pull the page out to swap or redesign it, which is handy for a kid who likes to remake their own chart. Whichever you choose, test your marker on a corner first, since some markers stain inexpensive laminate.

faq.q: Do magnetic chore charts actually work for adults?
faq.a: They can, if you treat the board as a way to get tasks out of your head and somewhere you'll actually see them. A wipe-clean chart on the fridge — or a sticky-note version where you physically move each note from "to do" to "done" — makes the size of the work visible and gives you steady, satisfying proof of progress. It's the same reason a posted chart beats a buried phone list: what's visible where you live is what gets done. The board is a tracker, though, not a motivator — the follow-through is still on you.
